title: Intake Completeness Validator
description: Recursive tree walk — a nested required-field schema (true = required leaf, object = required subtree); recurse to collect every missing required leaf as a dotted path, recursing into {} when a whole parent subtree is missing so its leaves still surface.

notes: Recursion is what handles arbitrary nesting depth: the schema can nest subtrees inside subtrees, and the same function walks any depth without hardcoding levels.

When a parent subtree is missing entirely (`insurance: null`), recurse into `{}` rather than skipping — so every required leaf beneath it (carrier, policyNumber) is reported individually, not just the parent.

Empty string counts as missing alongside null/undefined — a blank text field on the form is not a filled field. Use `=== ''` explicitly; a truthiness check would also reject `0` or `false`, which are valid values for other field types.

questions.q: Why is recursion the right tool for validating this schema?
options: Recursion is always faster than loops
The schema nests subtrees to arbitrary depth, and one recursive function walks any depth without hardcoding the levels
questions.explain: A subtree can contain subtrees; recursion descends each level uniformly instead of writing a fixed number of nested loops.

questions.q: When `insurance: null` (a whole required subtree is missing), why recurse into `{}` instead of just reporting `insurance`?
options: To avoid a crash from reading properties of null
So every required leaf under it (carrier, policyNumber) is reported individually, telling the user exactly which fields to fill
It is a no-op; the recursion returns nothing
questions.explain: Recursing into {} makes each child read as missing, so the report names every concrete field the user must supply, not just the group.

questions.q: Why does the validator treat an empty string `''` as missing?
options: A blank form field is not a filled field, so a required field left empty must be flagged
All falsy values should be rejected
questions.explain: The user typed nothing into a required box. Note it checks `=== ''` explicitly rather than truthiness, so valid `0`/`false` values on other field types are not wrongly flagged.

questions.q: Why does the code read `data == null ? undefined : data[key]` instead of just `data[key]`?
options: To convert the value to a number
When recursing into a missing subtree, `data` is `{}` (safe) — but the guard also prevents a TypeError if a null/undefined ever reaches the read
questions.explain: Reading a property off null/undefined throws. The guard short-circuits to undefined so the leaf is reported as missing rather than crashing.

exercises.prompt: Build a dotted path from a prefix and a key — top-level keys have no dot. Fill the template literal and the falsy-or-empty check so the empty value is reported.
A required subtree is missing (val is null) — recurse into `{}` so its leaves still report. Fill the recursive call's data argument and the spread that flattens the returned paths.

blanks.hint: recurse into an empty object so children read as missing

L3.prompt: Given a nested required-field schema (true = required leaf, nested object = required subtree) and a submitted intake object, return the dotted paths of every missing required field. A field is missing if it's undefined, null, or ''. If a whole subtree's parent is missing, report each of its leaves. Print a header then each missing path as '- path'.
L3.expectedOutput:
Missing fields:
- dob
- incident.location
- insurance.carrier
- insurance.policyNumber
hints: Walk the schema keys. If the spec is `true`, it's a leaf — push the dotted path when the value is undefined/null/''.
If the spec is an object, it's a subtree — recurse with the value as the new data and the path as the new prefix.
When the subtree's value is null/undefined, recurse into `{}` instead, so every leaf beneath reports as missing rather than just the parent.
